title: Ἀετὸς ⟨τοξευθείς⟩
titleEn: The Eagle Shot with an Arrow
part: The Eagle Shot with an Arrow (Chambry 7 · Perry 276)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 7 (= Perry 276). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ὑπεράνωθεν πέτρας ἀετὸς ἐκαθέζετο λαγωοὺς θηρεῦσαι ζητῶν.
sentences.tr: Hyperanōthen petras aetos ekathezeto lagōous thēreusai zētōn.
sentences.l: High above a rock an eagle was sitting, seeking to hunt hares.
sentences.n: ἐκαθέζετο is imperfect — the tense that sets the scene and holds it open, while the aorists that follow fire off the events. ὑπεράνωθεν takes the genitive πέτρας.

sentences.t: Τοῦτον δέ τις ἔβαλε τοξεύσας, καὶ τὸ μὲν βέλος ἔσω εἰσῆλθεν· ἡ δὲ γλυφὶς σὺν τοῖς πτεροῖς πρὸ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν εἱστήκει.
sentences.tr: Touton de tis ebale toxeusas, kai to men belos esō eisēlthen: hē de glyphis syn tois pterois pro tōn ophthalmōn heistēkei.
sentences.l: And someone struck him, having shot with the bow, and the shaft went inside, while the notch, with its feathers, stood before his eyes.
sentences.i: Someone shot him with an arrow: the shaft drove in, while the notched end with its feathers stood before his eyes.
sentences.n: μέν … δέ sets the two halves of the arrow against each other; English usually carries it with no more than a “while.” ἔσω εἰσῆλθεν doubles the idea — “went in, inward” — which English will not repeat. γλυφίς is the notch cut in the butt of the arrow for the bowstring — the fletched end, the part still outside. εἱστήκει is pluperfect of ἵστημι with plain past sense, “was standing.”

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ ἰδὼν ἔφη· « Καὶ τοῦτό μοι ἑτέρα λύπη, τὸ τοῖς ἐμοῖς πτεροῖς ἀποθνῄσκειν. »
sentences.tr: Ho de idōn ephē: « Kai touto moi hetera lypē, to tois emois pterois apothnēiskein. »
sentences.l: And he, having seen it, said: « This too is another grief to me — the dying by my own feathers. »
sentences.i: Seeing it he said, « Here is a second grief for me: to die by my own feathers. »
sentences.n: τὸ … ἀποθνῄσκειν is the articular infinitive: the article turns the whole phrase into a noun, “the dying.” Greek names actions this way constantly where English would use a gerund. The dative πτεροῖς is instrumental, “by means of.”

sentences.t: Ὅτι τὸ κέντρον τῆς λύπης δεινότερόν ἐστιν, ὅταν τις ἐκ τῶν οἰκείων κινδυνεύσῃ.
sentences.tr: Hoti to kentron tēs lypēs deinoteron estin, hotan tis ek tōn oikeiōn kindyneusēi.
sentences.l: That the sting of grief is more terrible, whenever someone runs into danger from what is his own.
sentences.i: Grief stings the more sharply when the danger comes from one's own.
sentences.n: τῶν οἰκείων can be read either way and the Greek does not decide it: masculine, “one's own household and kin,” or neuter, “one's own things” — which would point straight back at the eagle's own feathers. The English is left open on purpose. ὅταν with the subjunctive (κινδυνεύσῃ) states the general case: “whenever it happens that…”
